tagline.text: The surf capital of the north, where waves, sunsets, and cafes come together

image.credit: Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Emman Asuncion Foronda / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A beach town in La Union known as "the surfing capital of Northern Luzon." Waves gentle enough for beginners to stand on a board after just an hour's lesson, sunsets that sink into the South China Sea, and the cafes and restaurants opened by surfers have made it the favorite weekend getaway of young Manileños.
San Juan is a west-coast town about
270km

from Manila, just north of San Fernando, the capital of La Union province. Along the coastal North Luzon road (MacArthur Highway), Urbiztondo Beach stretches for several kilometers, densely packed with surf schools, guesthouses, and cafes. Filipinos shorten La Union to "LU," and it's become almost a ritual to take the Friday night bus in, ride waves all weekend, and head back.

The area is said to have become a surfing destination after Americans stationed at a nearby U.S. military facility started riding the waves in the 1960s and '70s. Local young people later learned to surf and became instructors themselves, and today the whole town runs on surfing. In
, the surfing events of the Southeast Asian Games (SEA Games) were even held at San Juan's Monaliza Point.

Urbiztondo Beach has a sandy bottom with waves that break evenly, making it good for beginners to learn, while Monaliza Point to the south draws experienced surfers with a right-hand break over a rocky bottom. Even if you don't surf, it's a great place to sit on the sand and watch the sunset, or wander between cafes and bars at an easy pace.

It suits travelers who want to learn to surf for the first time, those looking for a stopover between Baguio and Vigan, and younger travelers who prefer a lively beach scene over a quiet retreat. If you're hoping for open-water swimming and snorkeling, it may disappoint compared to the clear waters of the Visayan islands, so it's best to come thinking of it as a place for surfing and atmosphere rather than swimming.
Surf schools line the beach, and a one-on-one lesson with an instructor, including board rental, runs about
per
hour
. Most people manage to stand up on the board during their very first lesson.
Because the beach faces west, you get a direct view of the sun setting into the South China Sea. At dusk, surfers and travelers sit together on the sand to watch the sky turn red.
A reef break south of San Juan where big, fast waves draw experienced surfers. Even if you're not riding it yourself, it's fun to watch top-level surfers ride from the shore.
Coffee shops and brunch spots opened by surfers cluster along the beach road. El Union Coffee, famous for its cold brew, is often credited with starting San Juan's cafe culture.
A Taoist temple atop a hill in San Fernando, about
15–20 minutes
by car. Its red roofs and towers are striking, and it overlooks downtown San Fernando and the sea, making it a great photo spot.

blocks.title: A day trip to Tangadan Falls

children.text: An inland waterfall in San Gabriel, reachable from San Juan in a half day combining a drive and a short trek. A good alternative for a day when the waves are calm.
San Fernando's Halo-halo de Iloko is famous for its generous toppings of ube and leche flan. Be sure to also try grilled corn from beach stalls and Ilocano-style empanada.
On weekend nights, beach bars and hostels host acoustic sets or DJ parties. If you want a quiet stay, choose lodging a bit north of Urbiztondo's busy center.

After lunch, catch a bus back to Manila or head onward to Vigan or Baguio
The easiest way is to take a Partas bus bound for Vigan or Laoag from the Cubao or Pasay terminal in Manila and get off at San Juan Urbiztondo. It takes about
5–7 hours
, for a one-way fare of about
. Northbound buses from Viron, Dominion, and others also pass along the coastal road, so let the driver know in advance that you're getting off at San Juan.
For a more comfortable seat, take a premium bus like Joybus (Genesis) to San Fernando, then continue about
15–20 minutes
by jeepney or tricycle. Weekend buses often sell out by Friday night, so booking online is recommended.
From Baguio, buses and vans to San Fernando (La Union) run frequently, taking about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
for a fare of about
Take NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX to the Rosario exit, then head north along the coastal road. Without traffic it takes about
4–5 hours
, though leaving Friday evening on a weekend can take
6 hours
or more. Most beachfront accommodations have parking, but spaces are tight, so confirm when booking.
San Fernando has a small airport, but it has almost no scheduled passenger flights. Coming from Korea, it's most practical to land at Clark International Airport (CRK) and drive about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours
, or fly into Laoag International Airport (LAO) and drive south about
4–5 hours
Jeepneys run frequently along the beach road into downtown San Fernando for about
. For short distances, take a tricycle (short trips about
); on a day when you're combining the falls and the temple, chartering a tricycle or van for the whole day is more convenient.
The best time to surf is
October–March
, when the northeast monsoon (Amihan) blows. Waves arrive steadily and the weather stays cool, making it enjoyable for both beginners and experienced surfers, with
December–February
especially pleasant at around
. If you're only planning to relax on the beach, the drier
November–May
period is good, and in
April–May
the waves grow smaller, which is easier for beginners to practice on, though midday temperatures run very hot.
June–September

is the rainy season, affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons. Big swells before and after a typhoon can be an opportunity for experienced surfers, but they're dangerous for beginners, and the coastal road sometimes gets cut off. During Holy Week, the year-end holidays, and weekends with surf competitions, lodging sells out early, so book ahead.

Accommodations cluster along the Urbiztondo beach road. Hostel dorms where surfers gather run about
a night, guesthouses with private rooms about
, and pool resorts about

. San Juan Surf Resort, run by the Landrigan family, pioneers of Philippine surfing, is a long-established landmark stay and surf school. If you want a quiet place late at night, avoid the bar-heavy center of town.

True to its surfer-town character, the food scene mixes Western-style brunches, burgers, and tacos with local Filipino dishes. Be sure to try bagnet, the crispy deep-fried pork belly of the Ilocos region, pinakbet, a vegetable stew, and the orange, rice-flour-crusted empanada. Halo-halo de Iloko in San Fernando is popular enough to draw long lines, and beach stalls sell grilled corn and coconut juice around sunset. For souvenirs, northern specialties like Ilocos vinegar and chicharon corn snacks make good gifts.
For beginners, the best time for a lesson is
6–9 AM
, when the wind is light and the waves are even. Wind picks up and the sun grows stronger by midday.
Before your lesson, ask your instructor about their experience, rates, and board size, and start with a long, high-buoyancy soft-top board.
A rash guard and reef-safe sunscreen help reduce chafing and sunburn.
Friday night through Sunday brings a rush of travelers from Manila. Visit on a weekday for a quieter experience.
There are a few ATMs along the San Juan beach road, but they often run out of cash. Withdraw plenty in downtown San Fernando beforehand.
Weekend buses back to Manila tend to sell out by Sunday afternoon, so book your return ticket in advance.
Since San Juan sits roughly midway between Baguio and Vigan, it pairs well into a Northern Luzon loop route of Baguio–San Juan–Vigan.

Some stretches of Urbiztondo develop rip currents (fast currents pulling out to sea). Avoid swimming on high-wave days or when a red flag is flying, and beginners should always go in with an instructor.
Monaliza Point has a bottom of rock and coral, and beginners entering the water there risk serious injury.
While surfing, follow basic etiquette such as not dropping in on another surfer's wave, and always wear a leash in crowded areas so you don't lose your board.
Vehicles and buses move quickly along the beach road. Be especially careful crossing at night.
Don't leave your belongings on the beach while you're in the water — leave valuables in your accommodation's safe or a surf school locker instead.
If a typhoon warning is issued, the coastal road and bus service may be cut off, so check the weather forecast regularly.
